directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Egremont Russet is partially self-fertile but crops best with a compatible pollinator, and it is one of the more reliably disease-resistant older English apples. The most widely grown and best-known russet apple in Britain, dating to the nineteenth century, it bears medium, dull golden-brown, rough-skinned fruit with dense, crisp, distinctively nutty, slightly sweet flesh that is prized by connoisseurs and pairs especially well with cheese. Its good resistance to scab and canker compared to many other classic English apples has kept it a popular, relatively trouble-free choice for a home orchard wanting a true old-fashioned russet apple. Harvest in early-to-mid fall and eat fresh from the tree or after a short period of storage, since russet apples generally do not keep as long as some smooth-skinned dessert varieties.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Discovery is one of the earliest apples of the season and does not store for long once picked. Bred in Essex, England in the mid-twentieth century, this bright red, crisp early-season apple is prized for being one of the first dessert apples ready to eat each year, typically harvested in late summer well ahead of most other varieties, with crisp, juicy, mildly sweet-tart white flesh that occasionally shows an attractive pink-tinged blush just under the skin. Its early ripening and reliable, moderate cropping have made it a popular home garden choice for gardeners eager for the first fresh apple of the season, though the fruit is best eaten within a few weeks of picking rather than stored long-term. Harvest in mid-to-late summer as soon as fruit colors up and pulls easily from the spur, and eat promptly for the best crisp texture and flavor.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; James Grieve is a reliable, heavy-blooming pollinator for many other mid-season apple varieties. Bred in Edinburgh, Scotland in the late nineteenth century, it bears medium, yellow-green apples flushed with red stripes and juicy, tender, well-balanced sweet-tart flesh good for both fresh eating and cooking, ripening in late summer to early fall as one of the more reliable early-to-mid-season dual-purpose apples for a cooler climate. Its good cold hardiness, heavy and reliable annual bearing, and value as a strong cross-pollinator for many other apple varieties have kept it a widely planted favorite in home orchards across the British Isles and other cool-summer regions for well over a century. Harvest in late summer once fruit colors up and pulls easily from the spur, and eat within a few weeks, since the tender flesh does not store especially long.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Worcester Pearmain ripens in late summer and is best eaten promptly, since it does not store for long. Bred in Worcestershire, England in the nineteenth century, it bears bright crimson-red, medium apples with crisp, white flesh carrying a distinctive light strawberry-like aroma and flavor that sets it apart from most other dessert apples, ripening in late summer as one of the more colorful and distinctively flavored early-season varieties. Its attractive bright color and unusual, well-loved fruity flavor have made it a longstanding favorite for fresh eating straight from the tree, though the fruit softens and loses its best texture within just a few weeks of harvest. Harvest in late summer once fruit colors up fully and pulls easily from the spur, and eat promptly for the best crisp texture and distinctive flavor.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Blenheim Orange is a triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it cannot pollinate other apples and needs two different diploid varieties nearby.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Blenheim Orange is a triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it cannot pollinate other apples and needs two different diploid varieties nearby. An old English variety dating to the eighteenth century, it bears large, handsome, orange-red-flushed apples with dry, nutty, richly flavored flesh good for both fresh eating once fully ripe and for cooking, one of the classic dual-purpose apples that bridges the line between dessert and culinary use. As a triploid, it produces sterile pollen and requires two other diploid apple varieties planted nearby for reliable cross-pollination of itself and each other, a detail worth planning for before planting, and it makes a large, vigorous, long-lived tree. Harvest in mid-fall and let the fruit mellow in storage for a few weeks before eating fresh, since the flesh is at its best after a short period off the tree.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Bramley's Seedling is a vigorous, triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it needs two different diploid varieties nearby and ample permanent space.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Bramley's Seedling is a vigorous, triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it needs two different diploid varieties nearby and ample permanent space. Grown from a pip planted in Nottinghamshire, England around 1809, this is the definitive British culinary apple, producing very large, bright green, sharply tart fruit that cooks down into a smooth, fluffy puree prized above nearly all other apples for pies, sauces, and traditional English cooking, though it is far too acidic and firm-fleshed for most people's taste eaten fresh off the tree. As a triploid it produces sterile pollen and needs two other diploid apple varieties planted nearby for cross-pollination, and it makes a notably large, vigorous, long-lived tree that benefits from ample permanent space and a sturdy semi-standard or standard rootstock. Harvest in mid-to-late fall once fully ripe, and the acidic fruit stores exceptionally well through winter when kept cool, making it a valued keeper for a home cook's cooking apple supply.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Laxton's Superb is a reliable, cold-hardy alternative to Cox's Orange Pippin for gardeners wanting similar flavor from a more forgiving tree.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Laxton's Superb is a reliable, cold-hardy alternative to Cox's Orange Pippin for gardeners wanting similar flavor from a more forgiving tree. Bred in Bedfordshire, England in the early twentieth century from a Cox's Orange Pippin and Wyken Pippin cross, it bears medium, red-flushed russeted apples with rich, aromatic, well-balanced sweet-tart flesh reminiscent of its famous Cox parent, but on a tree that is notably hardier, more reliably productive, and more forgiving of less-than-ideal growing conditions than the notoriously finicky Cox. Its combination of excellent Cox-like flavor and much easier garden performance has made it a favored choice for gardeners wanting classic English dessert apple flavor without Cox's demanding cultural requirements. Harvest in mid-fall and store for a few weeks to a couple of months, during which the flavor continues to develop and improve.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Ellison's Orange ripens in late summer to early fall and is best eaten within a few weeks of harvest.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Ellison's Orange ripens in late summer to early fall and is best eaten within a few weeks of harvest. Bred in Lincolnshire, England from Cox's Orange Pippin parentage, it bears medium, yellow-green apples flushed with red and carrying rich, aromatic flesh with a distinctive light aniseed note layered over classic Cox-like sweetness, a flavor combination that has made it a favorite among English apple enthusiasts seeking something a bit different from the standard dessert apple. It ripens earlier in the season than its famous Cox parent and is a somewhat easier, more forgiving tree to grow well, making Cox-like flavor accessible to gardeners without ideal conditions for true Cox's Orange Pippin. Harvest in early-to-mid fall once fruit colors up and pulls easily from the spur, and eat within a few weeks for the best distinctive aromatic flavor.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Spartan is a cold-hardy, reliably productive apple well suited to northern climates. Bred in British Columbia, Canada in the 1920s from a McIntosh and Yellow Newtown Pippin cross, it bears medium, deep purple-red apples with crisp, snow-white, juicy flesh and a sweet flavor with the light, distinctive tang inherited from its McIntosh parent, ripening in early-to-mid fall as a reliable, attractive dessert apple. Its excellent cold hardiness, reliable annual bearing, and good disease resistance compared to many other apples have made it a longstanding favorite for northern and Canadian home orchards where more tender varieties struggle. Harvest in early-to-mid fall once fruit colors up deeply and pulls easily from the spur, and expect good storage life of a couple of months under cool conditions.
